[737](https://docs.rs#737)    /// Manual hook which constructs `DefaultHandler`s.
[738](https://docs.rs#738)    ///
[739](https://docs.rs#739)    /// # Details
[740](https://docs.rs#740)    ///
[741](https://docs.rs#741)    /// When supplied to the `set_hook` function, `default_with` will cause `eyre::Report` to use
[742](https://docs.rs#742)    /// `DefaultHandler` as the error report handler.
[743](https://docs.rs#743)    ///
[744](https://docs.rs#744)    /// If the `auto-install` feature is enabled, and a user-provided hook for constructing
[745](https://docs.rs#745)    /// `EyreHandlers` was not installed using `set_hook`, `DefaultHandler::default_with`
[746](https://docs.rs#746)    /// is automatically installed as the hook.
[747](https://docs.rs#747)    ///
[748](https://docs.rs#748)    /// # Example
[749](https://docs.rs#749)    ///
[750](https://docs.rs#750)    /// ```rust,should_panic
[751](https://docs.rs#751)    /// use eyre::{DefaultHandler, eyre, InstallError, Result, set_hook};
[752](https://docs.rs#752)    ///
[753](https://docs.rs#753)    /// fn main() -> Result<()> {
[754](https://docs.rs#754)    ///     install_default().expect("default handler inexplicably already installed");
[755](https://docs.rs#755)    ///     Err(eyre!("hello from default error city!"))
[756](https://docs.rs#756)    /// }
[757](https://docs.rs#757)    ///
[758](https://docs.rs#758)    /// fn install_default() -> Result<(), InstallError> {
[759](https://docs.rs#759)    ///     set_hook(Box::new(DefaultHandler::default_with))
[760](https://docs.rs#760)    /// }
[761](https://docs.rs#761)    ///
[762](https://docs.rs#762)    /// ```
[763](https://docs.rs#763)    #[allow(unused_variables)]
[764](https://docs.rs#764)    #[cfg_attr(not(feature = "auto-install"), allow(dead_code))]
[765](https://docs.rs#765)    pub fn default_with(error: &(dyn StdError + 'static)) -> Box<dyn EyreHandler> {
[766](https://docs.rs#766)        let backtrace = backtrace_if_absent!(error);
[767](https://docs.rs#767)
[768](https://docs.rs#768)        Box::new(Self {
[769](https://docs.rs#769)            backtrace,
[770](https://docs.rs#770)            #[cfg(track_caller)]
[771](https://docs.rs#771)            location: None,
[772](https://docs.rs#772)        })
[773](https://docs.rs#773)    }

[790](https://docs.rs#790)impl EyreHandler for DefaultHandler {
[791](https://docs.rs#791)    fn debug(
[792](https://docs.rs#792)        &self,
[793](https://docs.rs#793)        error: &(dyn StdError + 'static),
[794](https://docs.rs#794)        f: &mut core::fmt::Formatter<'_>,
[795](https://docs.rs#795)    ) -> core::fmt::Result {
[796](https://docs.rs#796)        use core::fmt::Write as _;
[797](https://docs.rs#797)
[798](https://docs.rs#798)        if f.alternate() {
[799](https://docs.rs#799)            return core::fmt::Debug::fmt(error, f);
[800](https://docs.rs#800)        }
[801](https://docs.rs#801)
[802](https://docs.rs#802)        write!(f, "{}", error)?;
[803](https://docs.rs#803)
[804](https://docs.rs#804)        if let Some(cause) = error.source() {
[805](https://docs.rs#805)            write!(f, "\n\nCaused by:")?;
[806](https://docs.rs#806)            let multiple = cause.source().is_some();
[807](https://docs.rs#807)            for (n, error) in crate::chain::Chain::new(cause).enumerate() {
[808](https://docs.rs#808)                writeln!(f)?;
[809](https://docs.rs#809)                if multiple {
[810](https://docs.rs#810)                    write!(indenter::indented(f).ind(n), "{}", error)?;
[811](https://docs.rs#811)                } else {
[812](https://docs.rs#812)                    write!(indenter::indented(f), "{}", error)?;
[813](https://docs.rs#813)                }
[814](https://docs.rs#814)            }
[815](https://docs.rs#815)        }
[816](https://docs.rs#816)
[817](https://docs.rs#817)        #[cfg(all(track_caller, feature = "track-caller"))]
[818](https://docs.rs#818)        {
[819](https://docs.rs#819)            if let Some(location) = self.location {
[820](https://docs.rs#820)                write!(f, "\n\nLocation:\n")?;
[821](https://docs.rs#821)                write!(indenter::indented(f), "{}", location)?;
[822](https://docs.rs#822)            }
[823](https://docs.rs#823)        }
[824](https://docs.rs#824)
[825](https://docs.rs#825)        #[cfg(backtrace)]
[826](https://docs.rs#826)        {
[827](https://docs.rs#827)            use std::backtrace::BacktraceStatus;
[828](https://docs.rs#828)
[829](https://docs.rs#829)            let backtrace = self
[830](https://docs.rs#830)                .backtrace
[831](https://docs.rs#831)                .as_ref()
[832](https://docs.rs#832)                .or_else(|| error.backtrace())
[833](https://docs.rs#833)                .expect("backtrace capture failed");
[834](https://docs.rs#834)            if let BacktraceStatus::Captured = backtrace.status() {
[835](https://docs.rs#835)                write!(f, "\n\nStack backtrace:\n{}", backtrace)?;
[836](https://docs.rs#836)            }
[837](https://docs.rs#837)        }
[838](https://docs.rs#838)
[839](https://docs.rs#839)        Result::Ok(())
[840](https://docs.rs#840)    }
[841](https://docs.rs#841)
[842](https://docs.rs#842)    #[cfg(track_caller)]
[843](https://docs.rs#843)    fn track_caller(&mut self, location: &'static std::panic::Location<'static>) {
[844](https://docs.rs#844)        self.location = Some(location);
[845](https://docs.rs#845)    }

[872](https://docs.rs#872)
[873](https://docs.rs#873)/// type alias for `Result<T, Report>`
[874](https://docs.rs#874)///
[875](https://docs.rs#875)/// This is a reasonable return type to use throughout your application but also for `fn main`; if
[876](https://docs.rs#876)/// you do, failures will be printed along with a backtrace if one was captured.
[877](https://docs.rs#877)///
[878](https://docs.rs#878)/// `eyre::Result` may be used with one *or* two type parameters.
[879](https://docs.rs#879)///
[880](https://docs.rs#880)/// ```rust
[881](https://docs.rs#881)/// use eyre::Result;
[882](https://docs.rs#882)///
[883](https://docs.rs#883)/// # const IGNORE: &str = stringify! {
[884](https://docs.rs#884)/// fn demo1() -> Result<T> {...}
[885](https://docs.rs#885)///            // ^ equivalent to std::result::Result<T, eyre::Report>
[886](https://docs.rs#886)///
[887](https://docs.rs#887)/// fn demo2() -> Result<T, OtherError> {...}
[888](https://docs.rs#888)///            // ^ equivalent to std::result::Result<T, OtherError>
[889](https://docs.rs#889)/// # };
[890](https://docs.rs#890)/// ```
[891](https://docs.rs#891)///
[892](https://docs.rs#892)/// # Example
[893](https://docs.rs#893)///
[894](https://docs.rs#894)/// ```
[895](https://docs.rs#895)/// # pub trait Deserialize {}
[896](https://docs.rs#896)/// #
[897](https://docs.rs#897)/// # mod serde_json {
[898](https://docs.rs#898)/// #     use super::Deserialize;
[899](https://docs.rs#899)/// #     use std::io;
[900](https://docs.rs#900)/// #
[901](https://docs.rs#901)/// #     pub fn from_str<T: Deserialize>(json: &str) -> io::Result<T> {
[902](https://docs.rs#902)/// #         unimplemented!()
[903](https://docs.rs#903)/// #     }
[904](https://docs.rs#904)/// # }
[905](https://docs.rs#905)/// #
[906](https://docs.rs#906)/// # #[derive(Debug)]
[907](https://docs.rs#907)/// # struct ClusterMap;
[908](https://docs.rs#908)/// #
[909](https://docs.rs#909)/// # impl Deserialize for ClusterMap {}
[910](https://docs.rs#910)/// #
[911](https://docs.rs#911)/// use eyre::Result;
[912](https://docs.rs#912)///
[913](https://docs.rs#913)/// fn main() -> Result<()> {
[914](https://docs.rs#914)///     # return Ok(());
[915](https://docs.rs#915)///     let config = std::fs::read_to_string("cluster.json")?;
[916](https://docs.rs#916)///     let map: ClusterMap = serde_json::from_str(&config)?;
[917](https://docs.rs#917)///     println!("cluster info: {:#?}", map);
[918](https://docs.rs#918)///     Ok(())
[919](https://docs.rs#919)/// }
[920](https://docs.rs#920)/// ```
[921](https://docs.rs#921)pub type Result<T, E = Report> = core::result::Result<T, E>;
[922](https://docs.rs#922)
[923](https://docs.rs#923)/// Provides the `wrap_err` method for `Result`.
[924](https://docs.rs#924)///
[925](https://docs.rs#925)/// This trait is sealed and cannot be implemented for types outside of
[926](https://docs.rs#926)/// `eyre`.
[927](https://docs.rs#927)///
[928](https://docs.rs#928)/// # Example
[929](https://docs.rs#929)///
[930](https://docs.rs#930)/// ```
[931](https://docs.rs#931)/// use eyre::{WrapErr, Result};
[932](https://docs.rs#932)/// use std::fs;
[933](https://docs.rs#933)/// use std::path::PathBuf;
[934](https://docs.rs#934)///
[935](https://docs.rs#935)/// pub struct ImportantThing {
[936](https://docs.rs#936)///     path: PathBuf,
[937](https://docs.rs#937)/// }
[938](https://docs.rs#938)///
[939](https://docs.rs#939)/// impl ImportantThing {
[940](https://docs.rs#940)///     # const IGNORE: &'static str = stringify! {
[941](https://docs.rs#941)///     pub fn detach(&mut self) -> Result<()> {...}
[942](https://docs.rs#942)///     # };
[943](https://docs.rs#943)///     # fn detach(&mut self) -> Result<()> {
[944](https://docs.rs#944)///     #     unimplemented!()
[945](https://docs.rs#945)///     # }
[946](https://docs.rs#946)/// }
[947](https://docs.rs#947)///
[948](https://docs.rs#948)/// pub fn do_it(mut it: ImportantThing) -> Result<Vec<u8>> {
[949](https://docs.rs#949)///     it.detach().wrap_err("Failed to detach the important thing")?;
[950](https://docs.rs#950)///
[951](https://docs.rs#951)///     let path = &it.path;
[952](https://docs.rs#952)///     let content = fs::read(path)
[953](https://docs.rs#953)///         .wrap_err_with(|| format!("Failed to read instrs from {}", path.display()))?;
[954](https://docs.rs#954)///
[955](https://docs.rs#955)///     Ok(content)
[956](https://docs.rs#956)/// }
[957](https://docs.rs#957)/// ```
[958](https://docs.rs#958)///
[959](https://docs.rs#959)/// When printed, the outermost error would be printed first and the lower
[960](https://docs.rs#960)/// level underlying causes would be enumerated below.
[961](https://docs.rs#961)///
[962](https://docs.rs#962)/// ```console
[963](https://docs.rs#963)/// Error: Failed to read instrs from ./path/to/instrs.json
[964](https://docs.rs#964)///
[965](https://docs.rs#965)/// Caused by:
[966](https://docs.rs#966)///     No such file or directory (os error 2)
[967](https://docs.rs#967)/// ```
[968](https://docs.rs#968)///
[969](https://docs.rs#969)/// # Wrapping Types That Don't impl `Error` (e.g. `&str` and `Box<dyn Error>`)
[970](https://docs.rs#970)///
[971](https://docs.rs#971)/// Due to restrictions for coherence `Report` cannot impl `From` for types that don't impl
[972](https://docs.rs#972)/// `Error`. Attempts to do so will give "this type might implement Error in the future" as an
[973](https://docs.rs#973)/// error. As such, `wrap_err`, which uses `From` under the hood, cannot be used to wrap these
[974](https://docs.rs#974)/// types. Instead we encourage you to use the combinators provided for `Result` in `std`/`core`.
[975](https://docs.rs#975)///
[976](https://docs.rs#976)/// For example, instead of this:
[977](https://docs.rs#977)///
[978](https://docs.rs#978)/// ```rust,compile_fail
[979](https://docs.rs#979)/// use std::error::Error;
[980](https://docs.rs#980)/// use eyre::{WrapErr, Report};
[981](https://docs.rs#981)///
[982](https://docs.rs#982)/// fn wrap_example(err: Result<(), Box<dyn Error + Send + Sync + 'static>>) -> Result<(), Report> {
[983](https://docs.rs#983)///     err.wrap_err("saw a downstream error")
[984](https://docs.rs#984)/// }
[985](https://docs.rs#985)/// ```
[986](https://docs.rs#986)///
[987](https://docs.rs#987)/// We encourage you to write this:
[988](https://docs.rs#988)///
[989](https://docs.rs#989)/// ```rust
[990](https://docs.rs#990)/// use std::error::Error;
[991](https://docs.rs#991)/// use eyre::{WrapErr, Report, eyre};
[992](https://docs.rs#992)///
[993](https://docs.rs#993)/// fn wrap_example(err: Result<(), Box<dyn Error + Send + Sync + 'static>>) -> Result<(), Report> {
[994](https://docs.rs#994)///     err.map_err(|e| eyre!(e)).wrap_err("saw a downstream error")
[995](https://docs.rs#995)/// }
[996](https://docs.rs#996)/// ```
[997](https://docs.rs#997)///
[998](https://docs.rs#998)/// # Effect on downcasting
[999](https://docs.rs#999)///
[1000](https://docs.rs#1000)/// After attaching a message of type `D` onto an error of type `E`, the resulting
[1001](https://docs.rs#1001)/// `eyre::Report` may be downcast to `D` **or** to `E`.
[1002](https://docs.rs#1002)///
[1003](https://docs.rs#1003)/// That is, in codebases that rely on downcasting, Eyre's wrap_err supports
[1004](https://docs.rs#1004)/// both of the following use cases:
[1005](https://docs.rs#1005)///
[1006](https://docs.rs#1006)///   - **Attaching messages whose type is insignificant onto errors whose type
[1007](https://docs.rs#1007)///     is used in downcasts.**
[1008](https://docs.rs#1008)///
[1009](https://docs.rs#1009)///     In other error libraries whose wrap_err is not designed this way, it can
[1010](https://docs.rs#1010)///     be risky to introduce messages to existing code because new message might
[1011](https://docs.rs#1011)///     break existing working downcasts. In Eyre, any downcast that worked
[1012](https://docs.rs#1012)///     before adding the message will continue to work after you add a message, so
[1013](https://docs.rs#1013)///     you should freely wrap errors wherever it would be helpful.
[1014](https://docs.rs#1014)///
[1015](https://docs.rs#1015)///     ```
[1016](https://docs.rs#1016)///     # use eyre::bail;
[1017](https://docs.rs#1017)///     # use thiserror::Error;
[1018](https://docs.rs#1018)///     #
[1019](https://docs.rs#1019)///     # #[derive(Error, Debug)]
[1020](https://docs.rs#1020)///     # #[error("???")]
[1021](https://docs.rs#1021)///     # struct SuspiciousError;
[1022](https://docs.rs#1022)///     #
[1023](https://docs.rs#1023)///     # fn helper() -> Result<()> {
[1024](https://docs.rs#1024)///     #     bail!(SuspiciousError);
[1025](https://docs.rs#1025)///     # }
[1026](https://docs.rs#1026)///     #
[1027](https://docs.rs#1027)///     use eyre::{WrapErr, Result};
[1028](https://docs.rs#1028)///
[1029](https://docs.rs#1029)///     fn do_it() -> Result<()> {
[1030](https://docs.rs#1030)///         helper().wrap_err("Failed to complete the work")?;
[1031](https://docs.rs#1031)///         # const IGNORE: &str = stringify! {
[1032](https://docs.rs#1032)///         ...
[1033](https://docs.rs#1033)///         # };
[1034](https://docs.rs#1034)///         # unreachable!()
[1035](https://docs.rs#1035)///     }
[1036](https://docs.rs#1036)///
[1037](https://docs.rs#1037)///     fn main() {
[1038](https://docs.rs#1038)///         # #[cfg(not(feature = "auto-install"))]
[1039](https://docs.rs#1039)///         # eyre::set_hook(Box::new(eyre::DefaultHandler::default_with)).unwrap();
[1040](https://docs.rs#1040)///         let err = do_it().unwrap_err();
[1041](https://docs.rs#1041)///         if let Some(e) = err.downcast_ref::<SuspiciousError>() {
[1042](https://docs.rs#1042)///             // If helper() returned SuspiciousError, this downcast will
[1043](https://docs.rs#1043)///             // correctly succeed even with the message in between.
[1044](https://docs.rs#1044)///             # return;
[1045](https://docs.rs#1045)///         }
[1046](https://docs.rs#1046)///         # panic!("expected downcast to succeed");
[1047](https://docs.rs#1047)///     }
[1048](https://docs.rs#1048)///     ```
[1049](https://docs.rs#1049)///
[1050](https://docs.rs#1050)///   - **Attaching message whose type is used in downcasts onto errors whose
[1051](https://docs.rs#1051)///     type is insignificant.**
[1052](https://docs.rs#1052)///
[1053](https://docs.rs#1053)///     Some codebases prefer to use machine-readable messages to categorize
[1054](https://docs.rs#1054)///     lower level errors in a way that will be actionable to higher levels of
[1055](https://docs.rs#1055)///     the application.
[1056](https://docs.rs#1056)///
[1057](https://docs.rs#1057)///     ```
[1058](https://docs.rs#1058)///     # use eyre::bail;
[1059](https://docs.rs#1059)///     # use thiserror::Error;
[1060](https://docs.rs#1060)///     #
[1061](https://docs.rs#1061)///     # #[derive(Error, Debug)]
[1062](https://docs.rs#1062)///     # #[error("???")]
[1063](https://docs.rs#1063)///     # struct HelperFailed;
[1064](https://docs.rs#1064)///     #
[1065](https://docs.rs#1065)///     # fn helper() -> Result<()> {
[1066](https://docs.rs#1066)///     #     bail!("no such file or directory");
[1067](https://docs.rs#1067)///     # }
[1068](https://docs.rs#1068)///     #
[1069](https://docs.rs#1069)///     use eyre::{WrapErr, Result};
[1070](https://docs.rs#1070)///
[1071](https://docs.rs#1071)///     fn do_it() -> Result<()> {
[1072](https://docs.rs#1072)///         helper().wrap_err(HelperFailed)?;
[1073](https://docs.rs#1073)///         # const IGNORE: &str = stringify! {
[1074](https://docs.rs#1074)///         ...
[1075](https://docs.rs#1075)///         # };
[1076](https://docs.rs#1076)///         # unreachable!()
[1077](https://docs.rs#1077)///     }
[1078](https://docs.rs#1078)///
[1079](https://docs.rs#1079)///     fn main() {
[1080](https://docs.rs#1080)///         # #[cfg(not(feature = "auto-install"))]
[1081](https://docs.rs#1081)///         # eyre::set_hook(Box::new(eyre::DefaultHandler::default_with)).unwrap();
[1082](https://docs.rs#1082)///         let err = do_it().unwrap_err();
[1083](https://docs.rs#1083)///         if let Some(e) = err.downcast_ref::<HelperFailed>() {
[1084](https://docs.rs#1084)///             // If helper failed, this downcast will succeed because
[1085](https://docs.rs#1085)///             // HelperFailed is the message that has been attached to
[1086](https://docs.rs#1086)///             // that error.
[1087](https://docs.rs#1087)///             # return;
[1088](https://docs.rs#1088)///         }
[1089](https://docs.rs#1089)///         # panic!("expected downcast to succeed");
[1090](https://docs.rs#1090)///     }
[1091](https://docs.rs#1091)///     ```
[1092](https://docs.rs#1092)///
[1093](https://docs.rs#1093)/// # `wrap_err` vs `wrap_err_with`
[1094](https://docs.rs#1094)///
[1095](https://docs.rs#1095)/// `wrap_err` incurs a runtime cost even in the non-error case because it requires eagerly
[1096](https://docs.rs#1096)/// constructing the error object. `wrap_err_with` avoids this cost through lazy evaluation. This
[1097](https://docs.rs#1097)/// cost is proportional to the cost of the currently installed [`EyreHandler`]'s creation step.
[1098](https://docs.rs#1098)/// `wrap_err` is useful in cases where an constructed error object already exists.
[1099](https://docs.rs#1099)pub trait WrapErr<T, E>: context::private::Sealed {
[1100](https://docs.rs#1100)    /// Wrap the error value with a new adhoc error
[1101](https://docs.rs#1101)    #[cfg_attr(track_caller, track_caller)]
[1102](https://docs.rs#1102)    fn wrap_err<D>(self, msg: D) -> Result<T, Report>
[1103](https://docs.rs#1103)    where
[1104](https://docs.rs#1104)        D: Display + Send + Sync + 'static;
[1105](https://docs.rs#1105)
[1106](https://docs.rs#1106)    /// Wrap the error value with a new adhoc error that is evaluated lazily
[1107](https://docs.rs#1107)    /// only once an error does occur.
[1108](https://docs.rs#1108)    #[cfg_attr(track_caller, track_caller)]
[1109](https://docs.rs#1109)    fn wrap_err_with<D, F>(self, f: F) -> Result<T, Report>
[1110](https://docs.rs#1110)    where
[1111](https://docs.rs#1111)        D: Display + Send + Sync + 'static,
[1112](https://docs.rs#1112)        F: FnOnce() -> D;
[1113](https://docs.rs#1113)
[1114](https://docs.rs#1114)    /// Compatibility re-export of wrap_err for interop with `anyhow`
[1115](https://docs.rs#1115)    #[cfg_attr(track_caller, track_caller)]
[1116](https://docs.rs#1116)    fn context<D>(self, msg: D) -> Result<T, Report>
[1117](https://docs.rs#1117)    where
[1118](https://docs.rs#1118)        D: Display + Send + Sync + 'static;
[1119](https://docs.rs#1119)
[1120](https://docs.rs#1120)    /// Compatibility re-export of wrap_err_with for interop with `anyhow`
[1121](https://docs.rs#1121)    #[cfg_attr(track_caller, track_caller)]
[1122](https://docs.rs#1122)    fn with_context<D, F>(self, f: F) -> Result<T, Report>
[1123](https://docs.rs#1123)    where
[1124](https://docs.rs#1124)        D: Display + Send + Sync + 'static,
[1125](https://docs.rs#1125)        F: FnOnce() -> D;
[1126](https://docs.rs#1126)}
[1127](https://docs.rs#1127)
[1128](https://docs.rs#1128)/// Provides the [`ok_or_eyre`][OptionExt::ok_or_eyre] method for [`Option`].
[1129](https://docs.rs#1129)///
[1130](https://docs.rs#1130)/// This trait is sealed and cannot be implemented for types outside of
[1131](https://docs.rs#1131)/// `eyre`.
[1132](https://docs.rs#1132)///
[1133](https://docs.rs#1133)/// # Example
[1134](https://docs.rs#1134)///
[1135](https://docs.rs#1135)/// ```
[1136](https://docs.rs#1136)/// # #[cfg(not(feature = "auto-install"))]
[1137](https://docs.rs#1137)/// # eyre::set_hook(Box::new(eyre::DefaultHandler::default_with)).unwrap();
[1138](https://docs.rs#1138)/// use eyre::OptionExt;
[1139](https://docs.rs#1139)///
[1140](https://docs.rs#1140)/// let option: Option<()> = None;
[1141](https://docs.rs#1141)///
[1142](https://docs.rs#1142)/// let result = option.ok_or_eyre("static str error");
[1143](https://docs.rs#1143)///
[1144](https://docs.rs#1144)/// assert_eq!(result.unwrap_err().to_string(), "static str error");
[1145](https://docs.rs#1145)/// ```
[1146](https://docs.rs#1146)///
[1147](https://docs.rs#1147)/// # `ok_or_eyre` vs `ok_or_else`
[1148](https://docs.rs#1148)///
[1149](https://docs.rs#1149)/// If string interpolation is required for the generated [report][Report],
[1150](https://docs.rs#1150)/// use [`ok_or_else`][Option::ok_or_else] instead,
[1151](https://docs.rs#1151)/// invoking [`eyre!`] to perform string interpolation:
[1152](https://docs.rs#1152)///
[1153](https://docs.rs#1153)/// ```
[1154](https://docs.rs#1154)/// # #[cfg(not(feature = "auto-install"))]
[1155](https://docs.rs#1155)/// # eyre::set_hook(Box::new(eyre::DefaultHandler::default_with)).unwrap();
[1156](https://docs.rs#1156)/// use eyre::eyre;
[1157](https://docs.rs#1157)///
[1158](https://docs.rs#1158)/// let option: Option<()> = None;
[1159](https://docs.rs#1159)///
[1160](https://docs.rs#1160)/// let result = option.ok_or_else(|| eyre!("{} error", "dynamic"));
[1161](https://docs.rs#1161)///
[1162](https://docs.rs#1162)/// assert_eq!(result.unwrap_err().to_string(), "dynamic error");
[1163](https://docs.rs#1163)/// ```
[1164](https://docs.rs#1164)///
[1165](https://docs.rs#1165)/// `ok_or_eyre` incurs no runtime cost, as the error object
[1166](https://docs.rs#1166)/// is constructed from the provided static argument
[1167](https://docs.rs#1167)/// only in the `None` case.
[1168](https://docs.rs#1168)pub trait OptionExt<T>: context::private::Sealed {
[1169](https://docs.rs#1169)    /// Transform the [`Option<T>`] into a [`Result<T, E>`],
[1170](https://docs.rs#1170)    /// mapping [`Some(v)`][Option::Some] to [`Ok(v)`][Result::Ok]
[1171](https://docs.rs#1171)    /// and [`None`] to [`Report`].
[1172](https://docs.rs#1172)    ///
[1173](https://docs.rs#1173)    /// `ok_or_eyre` allows for eyre [`Report`] error objects
[1174](https://docs.rs#1174)    /// to be lazily created from static messages in the `None` case.
[1175](https://docs.rs#1175)    ///
[1176](https://docs.rs#1176)    /// For dynamic error messages, use [`ok_or_else`][Option::ok_or_else],
[1177](https://docs.rs#1177)    /// invoking [`eyre!`] in the closure to perform string interpolation.
[1178](https://docs.rs#1178)    fn ok_or_eyre<M>(self, message: M) -> crate::Result<T>
[1179](https://docs.rs#1179)    where
[1180](https://docs.rs#1180)        M: Debug + Display + Send + Sync + 'static;
[1181](https://docs.rs#1181)}
[1182](https://docs.rs#1182)
[1183](https://docs.rs#1183)/// Provides the `context` method for `Option` when porting from `anyhow`
[1184](https://docs.rs#1184)///
[1185](https://docs.rs#1185)/// This trait is sealed and cannot be implemented for types outside of
[1186](https://docs.rs#1186)/// `eyre`.
[1187](https://docs.rs#1187)///
[1188](https://docs.rs#1188)/// ## Why Doesn't `Eyre` impl `WrapErr` for `Option`?
[1189](https://docs.rs#1189)///
[1190](https://docs.rs#1190)/// `eyre` doesn't impl `WrapErr` for `Option` because `wrap_err` implies that you're creating a
[1191](https://docs.rs#1191)/// new error that saves the previous error as its `source`. Calling `wrap_err` on an `Option` is
[1192](https://docs.rs#1192)/// meaningless because there is no source error. `anyhow` avoids this issue by using a different
[1193](https://docs.rs#1193)/// mental model where you're adding "context" to an error, though this not a mental model for
[1194](https://docs.rs#1194)/// error handling that `eyre` agrees with.
[1195](https://docs.rs#1195)///
[1196](https://docs.rs#1196)/// Instead, `eyre` encourages users to think of each error as distinct, where the previous error
[1197](https://docs.rs#1197)/// is the context being saved by the new error, which is backwards compared to anyhow's model. In
[1198](https://docs.rs#1198)/// this model you're encouraged to use combinators provided by `std` for `Option` to convert an
[1199](https://docs.rs#1199)/// option to a `Result`
[1200](https://docs.rs#1200)///
[1201](https://docs.rs#1201)/// # Example
[1202](https://docs.rs#1202)///
[1203](https://docs.rs#1203)/// Instead of:
[1204](https://docs.rs#1204)///
[1205](https://docs.rs#1205)/// ```rust
[1206](https://docs.rs#1206)/// use eyre::ContextCompat;
[1207](https://docs.rs#1207)///
[1208](https://docs.rs#1208)/// fn get_thing(mut things: impl Iterator<Item = u32>) -> eyre::Result<u32> {
[1209](https://docs.rs#1209)///     things
[1210](https://docs.rs#1210)///         .find(|&thing| thing == 42)
[1211](https://docs.rs#1211)///         .context("the thing wasnt in the list")
[1212](https://docs.rs#1212)/// }
[1213](https://docs.rs#1213)/// ```
[1214](https://docs.rs#1214)///
[1215](https://docs.rs#1215)/// We encourage you to use this:
[1216](https://docs.rs#1216)///
[1217](https://docs.rs#1217)/// ```rust
[1218](https://docs.rs#1218)/// use eyre::eyre;
[1219](https://docs.rs#1219)///
[1220](https://docs.rs#1220)/// fn get_thing(mut things: impl Iterator<Item = u32>) -> eyre::Result<u32> {
[1221](https://docs.rs#1221)///     things
[1222](https://docs.rs#1222)///         .find(|&thing| thing == 42)
[1223](https://docs.rs#1223)///         .ok_or_else(|| eyre!("the thing wasnt in the list"))
[1224](https://docs.rs#1224)/// }
[1225](https://docs.rs#1225)/// ```
[1226](https://docs.rs#1226)pub trait ContextCompat<T>: context::private::Sealed {
[1227](https://docs.rs#1227)    /// Compatibility version of `wrap_err` for creating new errors with new source on `Option`
[1228](https://docs.rs#1228)    /// when porting from `anyhow`
[1229](https://docs.rs#1229)    #[cfg_attr(track_caller, track_caller)]
[1230](https://docs.rs#1230)    fn context<D>(self, msg: D) -> Result<T, Report>
[1231](https://docs.rs#1231)    where
[1232](https://docs.rs#1232)        D: Display + Send + Sync + 'static;
[1233](https://docs.rs#1233)
[1234](https://docs.rs#1234)    /// Compatibility version of `wrap_err_with` for creating new errors with new source on `Option`
[1235](https://docs.rs#1235)    /// when porting from `anyhow`
[1236](https://docs.rs#1236)    #[cfg_attr(track_caller, track_caller)]
[1237](https://docs.rs#1237)    fn with_context<D, F>(self, f: F) -> Result<T, Report>
[1238](https://docs.rs#1238)    where
[1239](https://docs.rs#1239)        D: Display + Send + Sync + 'static,
[1240](https://docs.rs#1240)        F: FnOnce() -> D;
[1241](https://docs.rs#1241)
[1242](https://docs.rs#1242)    /// Compatibility re-export of `context` for porting from `anyhow` to `eyre`
[1243](https://docs.rs#1243)    #[cfg_attr(track_caller, track_caller)]
[1244](https://docs.rs#1244)    fn wrap_err<D>(self, msg: D) -> Result<T, Report>
[1245](https://docs.rs#1245)    where
[1246](https://docs.rs#1246)        D: Display + Send + Sync + 'static;

# Report in eyre - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/eyre/0.6.12/eyre/struct.Report.html

`pub struct Report { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

The core error reporting type of the library, a wrapper around a dynamic error reporting type.

`Report` works a lot like `Box<dyn std::error::Error>`, but with these
differences:

- `Report`requires that the error is- `Send`,- `Sync`, and- `'static`.
- `Report`guarantees that a backtrace is available, even if the underlying error type does not provide one.
- `Report`is represented as a narrow pointer — exactly one word in size instead of two.

[§](https://docs.rs#display-representations)Display representations

When you print an error object using “{}” or to_string(), only the outermost underlying error is printed, not any of the lower level causes. This is exactly as if you had called the Display impl of the error from which you constructed your eyre::Report.

`Failed to read instrs from ./path/to/instrs.json`To print causes as well using eyre’s default formatting of causes, use the alternate selector “{:#}”.

`Failed to read instrs from ./path/to/instrs.json: No such file or directory (os error 2)`The Debug format “{:?}” includes your backtrace if one was captured. Note
that this is the representation you get by default if you return an error
from `fn main` instead of printing it explicitly yourself.

```
Error: Failed to read instrs from ./path/to/instrs.json
Caused by:
    No such file or directory (os error 2)
Stack backtrace:
   0: <E as eyre::context::ext::StdError>::ext_report
             at /git/eyre/src/backtrace.rs:26
   1: core::result::Result<T,E>::map_err
             at /git/rustc/src/libcore/result.rs:596
   2: eyre::context::<impl eyre::WrapErr<T,E,H> for core::result::Result<T,E>>::wrap_err_with
             at /git/eyre/src/context.rs:58
   3: testing::main
             at src/main.rs:5
   4: std::rt::lang_start
             at /git/rustc/src/libstd/rt.rs:61
   5: main
   6: __libc_start_main
   7: _start
```
To see a conventional struct-style Debug representation, use “{:#?}”.

```
Error {
    msg: "Failed to read instrs from ./path/to/instrs.json",
    source: Os {
        code: 2,
        kind: NotFound,
        message: "No such file or directory",
    },
}
```
If none of the built-in representations are appropriate and you would prefer
to render the error and its cause chain yourself, it can be done by defining
your own [ EyreHandler](https://docs.rs/trait.EyreHandler.html) and

[to use it.](https://docs.rs/fn.set_hook.html)

`hook`## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Create a new error object from any error type.

The error type must be threadsafe and `'static`, so that the `Report`
will be as well.

If the error type does not provide a backtrace, a backtrace will be created here to ensure that a backtrace exists.

Create a new error object from a printable error message.

If the argument implements std::error::Error, prefer `Report::new`
instead which preserves the underlying error’s cause chain and
backtrace. If the argument may or may not implement std::error::Error
now or in the future, use `eyre!(err)` which handles either way
correctly.

`Report::msg("...")` is equivalent to `eyre!("...")` but occasionally
convenient in places where a function is preferable over a macro, such
as iterator or stream combinators:

```
use eyre::{Report, Result};
use futures::stream::{Stream, StreamExt, TryStreamExt};
async fn demo<S>(stream: S) -> Result<Vec<Output>>
where
    S: Stream<Item = Input>,
{
    stream
        .then(ffi::do_some_work) // returns Result<Output, &str>
        .map_err(Report::msg)
        .try_collect()
        .await
}
```
Create a new error from an error message to wrap the existing error.

For attaching a higher level error message to a `Result` as it is propagated, the
[ WrapErr](https://docs.rs/trait.WrapErr.html) extension trait may be more convenient than this function.

The primary reason to use `error.wrap_err(...)` instead of `result.wrap_err(...)` via the
`WrapErr` trait would be if the message needs to depend on some data held by the underlying
error:

```
use eyre::Result;
use std::fs::File;
use std::path::Path;
struct ParseError {
    line: usize,
    column: usize,
}
fn parse_impl(file: File) -> Result<T, ParseError> {
    ...
}
pub fn parse(path: impl AsRef<Path>) -> Result<T> {
    let file = File::open(&path)?;
    parse_impl(file).map_err(|error| {
        let message = format!(
            "only the first {} lines of {} are valid",
            error.line, path.as_ref().display(),
        );
        eyre::Report::new(error).wrap_err(message)
    })
}
```
An iterator of the chain of source errors contained by this Report.

This iterator will visit every error in the cause chain of this error object, beginning with the error that this error object was created from.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use eyre::Report;
use std::io;
pub fn underlying_io_error_kind(error: &Report) -> Option<io::ErrorKind> {
    for cause in error.chain() {
        if let Some(io_error) = cause.downcast_ref::<io::Error>() {
            return Some(io_error.kind());
        }
    }
    None
}
```
Returns true if `E` is the type held by this error object.

For errors constructed from messages, this method returns true if `E` matches the type of
the message `D` **or** the type of the error on which the message has been attached. For
details about the interaction between message and downcasting, [see here](https://docs.rs/trait.WrapErr.html#effect-on-downcasting).

Attempt to downcast the error object to a concrete type.

# WrapErr in eyre - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/eyre/0.6.12/eyre/trait.WrapErr.html

pub trait WrapErr<T, E>: Sealed {
    // Required methods
    fn

             F: [FnOnce](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/function/trait.FnOnce.html)() -> D;
}## Expand description

Provides the `wrap_err` method for `Result`.

This trait is sealed and cannot be implemented for types outside of
`eyre`.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use eyre::{WrapErr, Result};
use std::fs;
use std::path::PathBuf;
pub struct ImportantThing {
    path: PathBuf,
}
impl ImportantThing {
    pub fn detach(&mut self) -> Result<()> {...}
}
pub fn do_it(mut it: ImportantThing) -> Result<Vec<u8>> {
    it.detach().wrap_err("Failed to detach the important thing")?;
    let path = &it.path;
    let content = fs::read(path)
        .wrap_err_with(|| format!("Failed to read instrs from {}", path.display()))?;
    Ok(content)
}
```
When printed, the outermost error would be printed first and the lower level underlying causes would be enumerated below.

```
Error: Failed to read instrs from ./path/to/instrs.json
Caused by:
    No such file or directory (os error 2)
```
[§](https://docs.rs#wrapping-types-that-dont-impl-error-eg-str-and-boxdyn-error)Wrapping Types That Don’t impl `Error` (e.g. `&str` and `Box<dyn Error>`)

Due to restrictions for coherence `Report` cannot impl `From` for types that don’t impl
`Error`. Attempts to do so will give “this type might implement Error in the future” as an
error. As such, `wrap_err`, which uses `From` under the hood, cannot be used to wrap these
types. Instead we encourage you to use the combinators provided for `Result` in `std`/`core`.

For example, instead of this:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use std::error::Error;
use eyre::{WrapErr, Report};
fn wrap_example(err: Result<(), Box<dyn Error + Send + Sync + 'static>>) -> Result<(), Report> {
    err.wrap_err("saw a downstream error")
}
```
We encourage you to write this:

```
use std::error::Error;
use eyre::{WrapErr, Report, eyre};
fn wrap_example(err: Result<(), Box<dyn Error + Send + Sync + 'static>>) -> Result<(), Report> {
    err.map_err(|e| eyre!(e)).wrap_err("saw a downstream error")
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#effect-on-downcasting)Effect on downcasting

After attaching a message of type `D` onto an error of type `E`, the resulting
`eyre::Report` may be downcast to `D` **or** to `E`.

That is, in codebases that rely on downcasting, Eyre’s wrap_err supports both of the following use cases:

-
**Attaching messages whose type is insignificant onto errors whose type is used in downcasts.**In other error libraries whose wrap_err is not designed this way, it can be risky to introduce messages to existing code because new message might break existing working downcasts. In Eyre, any downcast that worked before adding the message will continue to work after you add a message, so you should freely wrap errors wherever it would be helpful. `use eyre::{WrapErr, Result}; fn do_it() -> Result<()> { helper().wrap_err("Failed to complete the work")?; ... } fn main() { let err = do_it().unwrap_err(); if let Some(e) = err.downcast_ref::<SuspiciousError>() { // If helper() returned SuspiciousError, this downcast will // correctly succeed even with the message in between. } }`
-
**Attaching message whose type is used in downcasts onto errors whose type is insignificant.**Some codebases prefer to use machine-readable messages to categorize lower level errors in a way that will be actionable to higher levels of the application. `use eyre::{WrapErr, Result}; fn do_it() -> Result<()> { helper().wrap_err(HelperFailed)?; ... } fn main() { let err = do_it().unwrap_err(); if let Some(e) = err.downcast_ref::<HelperFailed>() { // If helper failed, this downcast will succeed because // HelperFailed is the message that has been attached to // that error. } }`

[§](https://docs.rs#wrap_err-vs-wrap_err_with)`wrap_err` vs `wrap_err_with`

`wrap_err` incurs a runtime cost even in the non-error case because it requires eagerly
constructing the error object. `wrap_err_with` avoids this cost through lazy evaluation. This
cost is proportional to the cost of the currently installed [ EyreHandler](https://docs.rs/trait.EyreHandler.html)’s creation step.

`wrap_err` is useful in cases where an constructed error object already exists.## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/eyre/lib.rs.html#1109-1112)#### fn [wrap_err_with](https://docs.rs#tymethod.wrap_err_with)<D, F>(self, f: F) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)<T, [Report](https://docs.rs/struct.Report.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/eyre/lib.rs.html#1109-1112)

#### fn [wrap_err_with](https://docs.rs#tymethod.wrap_err_with)<D, F>(self, f: F) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)<T, [Report](https://docs.rs/struct.Report.html)>

Wrap the error value with a new adhoc error that is evaluated lazily only once an error does occur.

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait is **not** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

# bail in eyre - Rust

macro_rules! bail {

    ($err:expr $(,)?) => { ... };
    ($fmt:expr, $($arg:tt)*) => { ... };
}
```
## Expand description

Return early with an error.

This macro is equivalent to `return Err(eyre!(<args>))`.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
if !has_permission(user, resource) {
    bail!("permission denied for accessing {}", resource);
}
```
```
#[derive(Error, Debug)]
enum ScienceError {
    #[error("recursion limit exceeded")]
    RecursionLimitExceeded,
    ...
}
if depth > MAX_DEPTH {
    bail!(ScienceError::RecursionLimitExceeded);
}
```

# ensure in eyre - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/eyre/0.6.12/eyre/macro.ensure.html

```
macro_rules! ensure {
    ($cond:expr $(,)?) => { ... };
    ($cond:expr, $msg:literal $(,)?) => { ... };
    ($cond:expr, $err:expr $(,)?) => { ... };
    ($cond:expr, $fmt:expr, $($arg:tt)*) => { ... };
}
```
## Expand description

Return early with an error if a condition is not satisfied.

This macro is equivalent to `if !$cond { return Err(eyre!(<other args>)); }`.

Analogously to `assert!`, `ensure!` takes a condition and exits the function
if the condition fails. Unlike `assert!`, `ensure!` returns an `eyre::Result`
rather than panicking.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

`ensure!(user == 0, "only user 0 is allowed");````
#[derive(Error, Debug)]
enum ScienceError {
    #[error("recursion limit exceeded")]
    RecursionLimitExceeded,
    ...
}
ensure!(depth <= MAX_DEPTH, ScienceError::RecursionLimitExceeded);
```

macro_rules! eyre {

    ($err:expr $(,)?) => { ... };

## Expand description

Construct an ad-hoc error from a string.

This evaluates to a `Report`. It can take either just a string, or a format
string with arguments. It also can take any custom type which implements
`Debug` and `Display`.

```
use eyre::{eyre, Result};
fn lookup(key: &str) -> Result<V> {

        return Err(eyre!("key length must be 16 characters, got {:?}", key));
    }
    // ...
}
```

# Chain in eyre - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/eyre/0.6.12/eyre/struct.Chain.html

`pub struct Chain<'a> { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

Iterator of a chain of source errors.

This type is the iterator returned by [ Report::chain](https://docs.rs/struct.Report.html#method.chain).

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use eyre::Report;
use std::io;
pub fn underlying_io_error_kind(error: &Report) -> Option<io::ErrorKind> {
    for cause in error.chain() {
        if let Some(io_error) = cause.downcast_ref::<io::Error>() {
            return Some(io_error.kind());
        }
    }
    None
}
```
## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Construct an iterator over a chain of errors via the `source` method

[§](https://docs.rs#example-1)Example

```
use std::error::Error;
use std::fmt::{self, Write};
use eyre::Chain;
use indenter::indented;
fn report(error: &(dyn Error + 'static), f: &mut fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> fmt::Result {
    let mut errors = Chain::new(error).enumerate();
    for (i, error) in errors {
        writeln!(f)?;
        write!(indented(f).ind(i), "{}", error)?;
    }
    Ok(())
}
```

# DefaultHandler in eyre - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/eyre/0.6.12/eyre/struct.DefaultHandler.html

`pub struct DefaultHandler { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

The default provided error report handler for `eyre::Report`.

On nightly this supports conditionally capturing a `std::backtrace::Backtrace` if the source
error did not already capture one.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/eyre/lib.rs.html#765-773)#### pub fn [default_with](https://docs.rs#method.default_with)(error: &(dyn [StdError](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/error/trait.Error.html) + 'static)) -> [Box](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/boxed/struct.Box.html)<dyn [EyreHandler](https://docs.rs/trait.EyreHandler.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/eyre/lib.rs.html#765-773)

#### pub fn [default_with](https://docs.rs#method.default_with)(error: &(dyn [StdError](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/error/trait.Error.html) + 'static)) -> [Box](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/boxed/struct.Box.html)<dyn [EyreHandler](https://docs.rs/trait.EyreHandler.html)>

Manual hook which constructs `DefaultHandler`s.

[§](https://docs.rs#details)Details

When supplied to the `set_hook` function, `default_with` will cause `eyre::Report` to use
`DefaultHandler` as the error report handler.

If the `auto-install` feature is enabled, and a user-provided hook for constructing
`EyreHandlers` was not installed using `set_hook`, `DefaultHandler::default_with`
is automatically installed as the hook.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use eyre::{DefaultHandler, eyre, InstallError, Result, set_hook};
fn main() -> Result<()> {
    install_default().expect("default handler inexplicably already installed");
    Err(eyre!("hello from default error city!"))
}
fn install_default() -> Result<(), InstallError> {
    set_hook(Box::new(DefaultHandler::default_with))
}
```

}## Expand description

Provides the `context` method for `Option` when porting from `anyhow`

This trait is sealed and cannot be implemented for types outside of
`eyre`.

[§](https://docs.rs#why-doesnt-eyre-impl-wraperr-for-option)Why Doesn’t `Eyre` impl `WrapErr` for `Option`?

`eyre` doesn’t impl `WrapErr` for `Option` because `wrap_err` implies that you’re creating a
new error that saves the previous error as its `source`. Calling `wrap_err` on an `Option` is
meaningless because there is no source error. `anyhow` avoids this issue by using a different
mental model where you’re adding “context” to an error, though this not a mental model for
error handling that `eyre` agrees with.

Instead, `eyre` encourages users to think of each error as distinct, where the previous error
is the context being saved by the new error, which is backwards compared to anyhow’s model. In
this model you’re encouraged to use combinators provided by `std` for `Option` to convert an
option to a `Result`

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

Instead of:

```
use eyre::ContextCompat;
fn get_thing(mut things: impl Iterator<Item = u32>) -> eyre::Result<u32> {
    things
        .find(|&thing| thing == 42)
        .context("the thing wasnt in the list")
}
```
We encourage you to use this:

```
use eyre::eyre;
fn get_thing(mut things: impl Iterator<Item = u32>) -> eyre::Result<u32> {
    things
        .find(|&thing| thing == 42)
        .ok_or_else(|| eyre!("the thing wasnt in the list"))
}
```

Error Report Handler trait for customizing `eyre::Report`

## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

Define the report format

Used to override the report format of `eyre::Report`

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use backtrace::Backtrace;
use eyre::EyreHandler;
use eyre::Chain;
use std::error::Error;
use indenter::indented;
pub struct Handler {
    backtrace: Backtrace,
}
impl EyreHandler for Handler {
    fn debug(
        &self,
        error: &(dyn Error + 'static),
        f: &mut core::fmt::Formatter<'_>,
    ) -> core::fmt::Result {
        use core::fmt::Write as _;
        if f.alternate() {
            return core::fmt::Debug::fmt(error, f);
        }
        write!(f, "{}", error)?;
        if let Some(cause) = error.source() {
            write!(f, "\n\nCaused by:")?;
            let multiple = cause.source().is_some();
            for (n, error) in Chain::new(cause).enumerate() {
                writeln!(f)?;
                if multiple {
                    write!(indented(f).ind(n), "{}", error)?;
                } else {
                    write!(indented(f), "{}", error)?;
                }
            }
        }
        let backtrace = &self.backtrace;
        write!(f, "\n\nStack backtrace:\n{:?}", backtrace)?;
        Ok(())
    }
}
```

# Ok in eyre - Rust

`pub fn Ok<T>(t: T) -> `[Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)<T>## Expand description

Equivalent to Ok::<_, eyre::Error>(value).

This simplifies creation of an eyre::Result in places where type inference
cannot deduce the `E` type of the result — without needing to write
`Ok::<_, eyre::Error>(value)`.

One might think that `eyre::Result::Ok(value)` would work in such cases
but it does not.

```
error[E0282]: type annotations needed for `std::result::Result<i32, E>`
  --> src/main.rs:11:13
   |
11 |     let _ = eyre::Result::Ok(1);
   |         -   ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ cannot infer type for type parameter `E` declared on the enum `Result`
   |         |
   |         consider giving this pattern the explicit type `std::result::Result<i32, E>`, where the type parameter `E` is specified

# set_hook in eyre - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/eyre/0.6.12/eyre/fn.set_hook.html

```
pub fn set_hook(
    hook:
```
[Box](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/boxed/struct.Box.html)<dyn [Fn](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/function/trait.Fn.html)(&(dyn [StdError](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/error/trait.Error.html) + 'static)) -> [Box](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/boxed/struct.Box.html)<dyn [EyreHandler](https://docs.rs/trait.EyreHandler.html)> + [Sync](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Sync.html) + [Send](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Send.html) + 'static>,
) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/type.Result.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.unit.html), [InstallError](https://docs.rs/struct.InstallError.html)>## Expand description

Install the provided error hook for constructing EyreHandlers when converting Errors to Reports

[§](https://docs.rs#details)Details

To customize the format and content of error reports from `eyre` you must
first define a new `EyreHandler` type to capture and store the extra context
and to define the format of how to display the chain of errors and this
stored context. Once this type has been defined you must also define a global
hook used to construct these handlers whenever `Report`s are constructed.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use backtrace::Backtrace;
use eyre::EyreHandler;
use std::error::Error;
use std::{fmt, iter};
fn main() -> eyre::Result<()> {
    // Install our custom eyre report hook for constructing our custom Handlers
    install().unwrap();
    // construct a report with, hopefully, our custom handler!
    let mut report = eyre::eyre!("hello from custom error town!");
    // manually set the custom msg for this report after it has been constructed
    if let Some(handler) = report.handler_mut().downcast_mut::<Handler>() {
        handler.custom_msg = Some("you're the best users, you know that right???");
    }
    // print that shit!!
    Err(report)
}
// define a handler that captures backtraces unless told not to
fn install() -> Result<(), impl Error> {
    let capture_backtrace = std::env::var("RUST_BACKWARDS_TRACE")
        .map(|val| val != "0")
        .unwrap_or(true);
    let hook = Hook { capture_backtrace };
    eyre::set_hook(Box::new(move |e| Box::new(hook.make_handler(e))))
}
struct Hook {
    capture_backtrace: bool,
}
impl Hook {
    fn make_handler(&self, _error: &(dyn Error + 'static)) -> Handler {
        let backtrace = if self.capture_backtrace {
            Some(Backtrace::new())
        } else {
            None
        };
        Handler {
            backtrace,
            custom_msg: None,
        }
    }
}
struct Handler {
    // custom configured backtrace capture
    backtrace: Option<Backtrace>,
    // customizable message payload associated with reports
    custom_msg: Option<&'static str>,
}
impl EyreHandler for Handler {
    fn debug(&self, error: &(dyn Error + 'static), f: &mut fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> fmt::Result {
        if f.alternate() {
            return fmt::Debug::fmt(error, f);
        }
        let errors = iter::successors(Some(error), |error| (*error).source());
        for (ind, error) in errors.enumerate() {
            write!(f, "\n{:>4}: {}", ind, error)?;
        }
        if let Some(backtrace) = self.backtrace.as_ref() {
            writeln!(f, "\n\nBacktrace:\n{:?}", backtrace)?;
        }
        if let Some(msg) = self.custom_msg.as_ref() {
            writeln!(f, "\n\n{}", msg)?;
        }
        Ok(())
    }
}
```

# Result in eyre - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/eyre/0.6.12/eyre/type.Result.html

## Expand description

type alias for `Result<T, Report>`

This is a reasonable return type to use throughout your application but also for `fn main`; if
you do, failures will be printed along with a backtrace if one was captured.

`eyre::Result` may be used with one *or* two type parameters.

```
use eyre::Result;
fn demo1() -> Result<T> {...}
           // ^ equivalent to std::result::Result<T, eyre::Report>
fn demo2() -> Result<T, OtherError> {...}
           // ^ equivalent to std::result::Result<T, OtherError>
```
[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use eyre::Result;
fn main() -> Result<()> {
    let config = std::fs::read_to_string("cluster.json")?;
    let map: ClusterMap = serde_json::from_str(&config)?;
    println!("cluster info: {:#?}", map);
    Ok(())
}
```
## Aliased Type[§](https://docs.rs#aliased-type)

`pub enum Result<T, E = `[Report](https://docs.rs/struct.Report.html)> {
    Ok(T),
    Err(E),
}

# eyre - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/eyre/latest/eyre/

## Expand description

This library provides [ eyre::Report](https://docs.rs/eyre/*/eyre/struct.Report.html), a trait object based
error handling type for easy idiomatic error handling and reporting in Rust
applications.

This crate is a fork of [ anyhow](https://github.com/dtolnay/anyhow)  with support for customized
error reports. For more details on customization, check out the docs on

[.](https://docs.rs/eyre/*/eyre/trait.EyreHandler.html)

`eyre::EyreHandler`[§](https://docs.rs#custom-report-handlers)Custom Report Handlers

The heart of this crate is its ability to swap out the Handler type to change what information is carried alongside errors and how the end report is formatted. This crate is meant to be used alongside companion crates that customize its behavior. Below is a list of known crates that export report handlers for eyre and short summaries of what features they provide.

- `stable-eyre`- `std`’s to- `backtrace-rs`’s so that it can be captured on stable. The report format is identical to- `DefaultHandler`’s report format.
- `color-eyre`- `backtrace::Backtrace`and a- `tracing_error::SpanTrace`. Provides a- `Section`trait for attaching warnings and suggestions to error reports. The end report is then pretty printed with the help of- `color-backtrace`- `color-spantrace`- `ansi_term`. Check out the README on- `color-eyre`
- `simple-eyre`- `EyreHandler`that captures no additional information, for when you do not wish to capture- `Backtrace`s with errors.
- `jane-eyre`- `color-eyre`.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage-recommendations-and-stability-considerations)Usage Recommendations and Stability Considerations

**We recommend users do not re-export types from this library as part their
own public API for libraries with external users.** The main reason for this
is that it will make your library API break if we ever bump the major version
number on eyre and your users upgrade the eyre version they use in their
application code before you upgrade your own eyre dep version 1.

However, even beyond this API stability hazard, there are other good reasons
to avoid using `eyre::Report` as your public error type.

- You export an undocumented error interface that is otherwise still
accessible via downcast, making it hard for users to react to specific
errors while not preventing them from depending on details you didn’t mean
to make part of your public API.
- This in turn makes the error types of all libraries you use a part of your public API as well, and makes changing any of those libraries into undetectable runtime breakage.

- If many of your errors are constructed from strings, you encourage your users to use string comparison for reacting to specific errors, which is brittle and turns updating error messages into potentially undetectable runtime breakage.

[§](https://docs.rs#details)Details

-
Use `Result<T, eyre::Report>`, or equivalently`eyre::Result<T>`, as the return type of any fallible function.Within the function, use `?`to easily propagate any error that implements the`std::error::Error`trait.`use eyre::Result; fn get_cluster_info() -> Result<ClusterMap> { let config = std::fs::read_to_string("cluster.json")?; let map: ClusterMap = serde_json::from_str(&config)?; Ok(map) }`
-
Wrap a lower level error with a new error created from a message to help the person troubleshooting understand the chain of failures that occurred. A low-level error like “No such file or directory” can be annoying to debug without more information about what higher level step the application was in the middle of. `use eyre::{WrapErr, Result}; fn main() -> Result<()> { ... it.detach().wrap_err("Failed to detach the important thing")?; let content = std::fs::read(path) .wrap_err_with(|| format!("Failed to read instrs from {}", path))?; ... }``Error: Failed to read instrs from ./path/to/instrs.json Caused by: No such file or directory (os error 2)`
-
Downcasting is supported and can be done by value, by shared reference, or by mutable reference as needed. `// If the error was caused by redaction, then return a // tombstone instead of the content. match root_cause.downcast_ref::<DataStoreError>() { Some(DataStoreError::Censored(_)) => Ok(Poll::Ready(REDACTED_CONTENT)), None => Err(error), }`
-
If using the nightly channel, a backtrace is captured and printed with the error if the underlying error type does not already provide its own. In order to see backtraces, they must be enabled through the environment variables described in `std::backtrace`- If you want panics and errors to both have backtraces, set
`RUST_BACKTRACE=1`;
- If you want only errors to have backtraces, set `RUST_LIB_BACKTRACE=1`;
- If you want only panics to have backtraces, set `RUST_BACKTRACE=1`and`RUST_LIB_BACKTRACE=0`.
 The tracking issue for this feature is [rust-lang/rust#53487](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/53487).
- If you want panics and errors to both have backtraces, set
-
Eyre works with any error type that has an impl of `std::error::Error`, including ones defined in your crate. We do not bundle a`derive(Error)`macro but you can write the impls yourself or use a standalone macro like[thiserror](https://github.com/dtolnay/thiserror).`use thiserror::Error; #[derive(Error, Debug)] pub enum FormatError { #[error("Invalid header (expected {expected:?}, got {found:?})")] InvalidHeader { expected: String, found: String, }, #[error("Missing attribute: {0}")] MissingAttribute(String), }`
-
One-off error messages can be constructed using the `eyre!`macro, which supports string interpolation and produces an`eyre::Report`.`return Err(eyre!("Missing attribute: {}", missing));`
-
On newer versions of the compiler (i.e. 1.58 and later) this macro also supports format args captures. `return Err(eyre!("Missing attribute: {missing}"));`

[§](https://docs.rs#no-std-support)No-std support

No-std support was removed in 2020 in [commit 608a16a](https://github.com/eyre-rs/eyre/pull/29/commits/608a16aa2c2c27eca6c88001cc94c6973c18f1d5) due to unaddressed upstream breakages.

[§](https://docs.rs#comparison-to-failure)Comparison to failure

The `eyre::Report` type works something like `failure::Error`, but unlike
failure ours is built around the standard library’s `std::error::Error` trait
rather than a separate trait `failure::Fail`. The standard library has adopted
the necessary improvements for this to be possible as part of [RFC 2504](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/blob/master/text/2504-fix-error.md).

[§](https://docs.rs#comparison-to-thiserror)Comparison to thiserror

Use `eyre` if you don’t think you’ll do anything with an error other than
report it. This is common in application code. Use `thiserror` if you think
you need an error type that can be handled via match or reported. This is
common in library crates where you don’t know how your users will handle
your errors.

[§](https://docs.rs#compatibility-with-anyhow)Compatibility with `anyhow`

This crate does its best to be usable as a drop in replacement of `anyhow` and
vice-versa by re-exporting all of the renamed APIs with the names used in
`anyhow`, though there are some differences still.

[§](https://docs.rs#context-and-option)`Context` and `Option`

As part of renaming `Context` to `WrapErr` we also intentionally do not
implement `WrapErr` for `Option`. This decision was made because `wrap_err`
implies that you’re creating a new error that saves the old error as its
`source`. With `Option` there is no source error to wrap, so `wrap_err` ends up
being somewhat meaningless.

Instead `eyre` offers [ OptionExt::ok_or_eyre](https://docs.rs/trait.OptionExt.html#tymethod.ok_or_eyre) to yield

*static*errors from

`None`,
and intends for users to use the combinator functions provided by
`std`, converting `Option`s to `Result`s, for *dynamic*errors. So where you would write this with anyhow:

```
use anyhow::Context;
let opt: Option<()> = None;
let result_static = opt.context("static error message");
let result_dynamic = opt.with_context(|| format!("{} error message", "dynamic"));
```
With `eyre` we want users to write:

```
use eyre::{eyre, OptionExt, Result};
let opt: Option<()> = None;
let result_static: Result<()> = opt.ok_or_eyre("static error message");
let result_dynamic: Result<()> = opt.ok_or_else(|| eyre!("{} error message", "dynamic"));
```
**NOTE**: However, to help with porting we do provide a `ContextCompat` trait which
implements `context` for options which you can import to make existing
`.context` calls compile.

# indenter 0.3.4 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/indenter/^0.3.0

## indenter

A few wrappers for the `fmt::Write` objects that efficiently appends and remove
common indentation after every newline

## Setup

Add this to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "0.2"
```
## Examples

## Indentation only

This type is intended primarily for writing error reporters that gracefully format error messages that span multiple lines.

```
use Error;
use ;
use indented;
;
```
## "Dedenting" (removing common leading indendation)

This type is intended primarily for formatting source code. For example, when generating code.

This type requires the feature `std`.

```
use Error;
use ;
use CodeFormatter;
let mut output = Stringnew;
let mut f = new;
write!;
assert_eq!;
let mut output = Stringnew;
let mut f = new;
// it can also indent...
f.indent;
write!;
assert_eq!;
```

# Overview

`once_cell` provides two new cell-like types, `unsync::OnceCell` and `sync::OnceCell`. `OnceCell`
might store arbitrary non-`Copy` types, can be assigned to at most once and provide direct access
to the stored contents. In a nutshell, API looks *roughly* like this:

```
```
Note that, like with `RefCell` and `Mutex`, the `set` method requires only a shared reference.
Because of the single assignment restriction `get` can return an `&T` instead of `Ref<T>`
or `MutexGuard<T>`.

`once_cell` also has a `Lazy<T>` type, build on top of `OnceCell` which provides the same API as
the `lazy_static!` macro, but without using any macros:

```
use ;
use Lazy;
static GLOBAL_DATA:  = new;
```
More patterns and use-cases are in the [docs](https://docs.rs/once_cell/)!

# pyo3 0.20.3 - Docs.rs

# PyO3

[Rust](https://www.rust-lang.org/) bindings for [Python](https://www.python.org/), including tools for creating native Python extension modules. Running and interacting with Python code from a Rust binary is also supported.

## Usage

PyO3 supports the following software versions:

- Python 3.7 and up (CPython and PyPy)
- Rust 1.56 and up

You can use PyO3 to write a native Python module in Rust, or to embed Python in a Rust binary. The following sections explain each of these in turn.

### Using Rust from Python

PyO3 can be used to generate a native Python module. The easiest way to try this out for the first time is to use [ maturin](https://github.com/PyO3/maturin).

`maturin` is a tool for building and publishing Rust-based Python packages with minimal configuration. The following steps install `maturin`, use it to generate and build a new Python package, and then launch Python to import and execute a function from the package.First, follow the commands below to create a new directory containing a new Python `virtualenv`, and install `maturin` into the virtualenv using Python's package manager, `pip`:

```
# (replace string_sum with the desired package name)
```
Still inside this `string_sum` directory, now run `maturin init`. This will generate the new package source. When given the choice of bindings to use, select pyo3 bindings:

```

```
The most important files generated by this command are `Cargo.toml` and `lib.rs`, which will look roughly like the following:

`Cargo.toml`

```
[]
 = "string_sum"
 = "0.1.0"
 = "2021"
[]
# The name of the native library. This is the name which will be used in Python to import the
# library (i.e. `import string_sum`). If you change this, you must also change the name of the
# `#[pymodule]` in `src/lib.rs`.
 = "string_sum"
# "cdylib" is necessary to produce a shared library for Python to import from.
#
# Downstream Rust code (including code in `bin/`, `examples/`, and `tests/`) will not be able
# to `use string_sum;` unless the "rlib" or "lib" crate type is also included, e.g.:
# crate-type = ["cdylib", "rlib"]
 = ["cdylib"]
[]
 = {  = "0.20.3",  = ["extension-module"] }
```
`src/lib.rs`

```
use *;
/// Formats the sum of two numbers as string.
/// A Python module implemented in Rust. The name of this function must match
/// the `lib.name` setting in the `Cargo.toml`, else Python will not be able to
/// import the module.
```
Finally, run `maturin develop`. This will build the package and install it into the Python virtualenv previously created and activated. The package is then ready to be used from `python`:

```
# lots of progress output as maturin runs the compilation...
>>> import
>>> string_sum.sum_as_string()
```
To make changes to the package, just edit the Rust source code and then re-run `maturin develop` to recompile.

To run this all as a single copy-and-paste, use the bash script below (replace `string_sum` in the first command with the desired package name):

If you want to be able to run `cargo test` or use this project in a Cargo workspace and are running into linker issues, there are some workarounds in [the FAQ](https://pyo3.rs/latest/faq.html#i-cant-run-cargo-test-or-i-cant-build-in-a-cargo-workspace-im-having-linker-issues-like-symbol-not-found-or-undefined-reference-to-_pyexc_systemerror).

[manually](https://pyo3.rs/latest/building_and_distribution.html#manual-builds). Both offer more flexibility than

# anyhow 1.0.103 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/anyhow/^1.0.28

# Anyhow ¯\_(°ペ)_/¯

This library provides [ anyhow::Error](https://docs.rs/anyhow/1.0/anyhow/struct.Error.html), a trait object based error type
for easy idiomatic error handling in Rust applications.

```
[]
 = "1.0"
```
## Details

-
Use `Result<T, anyhow::Error>`, or equivalently`anyhow::Result<T>`, as the return type of any fallible function.Within the function, use `?`to easily propagate any error that implements the`std::error::Error``use Result;`
-
Attach context to help the person troubleshooting the error understand where things went wrong. A low-level error like "No such file or directory" can be annoying to debug without more context about what higher level step the application was in the middle of. `use ;``Error: Failed to read instrs from ./path/to/instrs.json Caused by: No such file or directory (os error 2)`
-
Downcasting is supported and can be by value, by shared reference, or by mutable reference as needed. `// If the error was caused by redaction, then return a // tombstone instead of the content. match root_cause.`
-
If using Rust ≥ 1.65, a backtrace is captured and printed with the error if the underlying error type does not already provide its own. In order to see backtraces, they must be enabled through the environment variables described in `std::backtrace`- If you want panics and errors to both have backtraces, set
`RUST_BACKTRACE=1`;
- If you want only errors to have backtraces, set `RUST_LIB_BACKTRACE=1`;
- If you want only panics to have backtraces, set `RUST_BACKTRACE=1`and`RUST_LIB_BACKTRACE=0`.

- If you want panics and errors to both have backtraces, set
-
Anyhow works with any error type that has an impl of `std::error::Error`, including ones defined in your crate. We do not bundle a`derive(Error)`macro but you can write the impls yourself or use a standalone macro like[thiserror](https://github.com/dtolnay/thiserror).`use Error;`
-
One-off error messages can be constructed using the `anyhow!`macro, which supports string interpolation and produces an`anyhow::Error`.`return Err;`A `bail!`macro is provided as a shorthand for the same early return.`bail!;`

## No-std support

In no_std mode, almost all of the same API is available and works the same way. To depend on Anyhow in no_std mode, disable our default enabled "std" feature in Cargo.toml. A global allocator is required.

```
[]
 = {  = "1.0",  = false }
```
With versions of Rust older than 1.81, no_std mode may require an additional
`.map_err(Error::msg)` when working with a non-Anyhow error type inside a
function that returns Anyhow's error type, as the trait that `?`-based error
conversions are defined by is only available in std in those old versions.

## Comparison to failure

The `anyhow::Error` type works something like `failure::Error`, but unlike
failure ours is built around the standard library's `std::error::Error` trait
rather than a separate trait `failure::Fail`. The standard library has adopted
the necessary improvements for this to be possible as part of [RFC 2504](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/blob/master/text/2504-fix-error.md).

## Comparison to thiserror

Use Anyhow if you don't care what error type your functions return, you just
want it to be easy. This is common in application code. Use [thiserror](https://github.com/dtolnay/thiserror) if you
are a library that wants to design your own dedicated error type(s) so that on
failures the caller gets exactly the information that you choose.

```
use Backtrace;
```
If, however, you'd like more raw access to the actual tracing functionality, you
can use the `trace` and `resolve` functions directly.

```
```
# Supported Rust Versions

The `backtrace` crate is a core component of the standard library, and must
at times keep up with the evolution of various platforms in order to serve
the standard library's needs. This often means using recent libraries
that provide unwinding and symbolication for various platforms.
Thus `backtrace` is likely to use recent Rust features or depend on a library
which itself uses them. Its minimum supported Rust version, by policy, is
within a few versions of current stable, approximately "stable - 2".

This policy takes precedence over versions written anywhere else in this repo.

# rustversion 1.0.22 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rustversion/^1.0

# Compiler version cfg

This crate provides macros for conditional compilation according to rustc
compiler version, analogous to [ #[cfg(...)]](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/conditional-compilation.html#the-cfg-attribute) and

[.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/conditional-compilation.html#the-cfg_attr-attribute)

`#[cfg_attr(...)]````
[]
 = "1.0"
```
## Selectors

-
`#[rustversion::stable]`— True on any stable compiler.
-
`#[rustversion::stable(1.34)]`— True on exactly the specified stable compiler.
-
`#[rustversion::beta]`— True on any beta compiler.
-
`#[rustversion::nightly]`— True on any nightly compiler or dev build.
-
`#[rustversion::nightly(2025-01-01)]`— True on exactly one nightly.
-
`#[rustversion::since(1.34)]`— True on that stable release and any later compiler, including beta and nightly.
-
`#[rustversion::since(2025-01-01)]`— True on that nightly and all newer ones.
-
`#[rustversion::before(`version or date`)]`— Negative of*#[rustversion::since(...)]*.
-
`#[rustversion::not(`selector`)]`— Negative of any selector; for example*#[rustversion::not(nightly)]*.
-
`#[rustversion::any(`selectors...`)]`— True if any of the comma-separated selectors is true; for example*#[rustversion::any(stable, beta)]*.
-
`#[rustversion::all(`selectors...`)]`— True if all of the comma-separated selectors are true; for example*#[rustversion::all(since(1.31), before(1.34))]*.
-
`#[rustversion::attr(`selector`,`attribute`)]`— For conditional inclusion of attributes; analogous to`cfg_attr`.
-
`rustversion::cfg!(`selector`)`— An expression form of any of the above attributes; for example*if rustversion::cfg!(any(stable, beta)) { ... }*.

## Use cases

Providing additional trait impls as types are stabilized in the standard library
without breaking compatibility with older compilers; in this case Pin<P>
stabilized in [Rust 1.33](https://blog.rust-lang.org/2019/02/28/Rust-1.33.0.html#pinning):

```

```
Similar but for language features; the ability to control alignment greater than
1 of packed structs was stabilized in [Rust 1.33](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/master/RELEASES.md#version-1330-2019-02-28).

```
;
```
Augmenting code with `const` as const impls are stabilized in the standard
library. This use of `const` as an attribute is recognized as a special case by
the rustversion::attr macro.

```
use Duration;
```
Emitting Cargo cfg directives from a build script. Note that this requires
listing `rustversion` under `[build-dependencies]` in Cargo.toml, not
`[dependencies]`.

```

```
