Mutably borrows an `Either` of `Iterator`s to be an `Iterator` of `Either`s

Unlike [ iter_mut](https://docs.rs/enum.Either.html#method.iter_mut), this does not require the

`Left` and `Right` iterators to have the same item type.```
use either::*;
let mut left: Either<_, Vec<u8>> = Left(["hello"]);
left.factor_iter_mut().for_each(|x| *x.unwrap_left() = "goodbye");
assert_eq!(left, Left(["goodbye"]));
let mut right: Either<[&str; 2], _> = Right(vec![0, 1, 2]);
right.factor_iter_mut().for_each(|x| if let Right(r) = x { *r = -*r; });
assert_eq!(right, Right(vec![0, -1, -2]));
```
Return left value or given value

Arguments passed to `left_or` are eagerly evaluated; if you are passing
the result of a function call, it is recommended to use
[ left_or_else](https://docs.rs/enum.Either.html#method.left_or_else), which is lazily evaluated.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
let left: Either<&str, &str> = Left("left");
assert_eq!(left.left_or("foo"), "left");
let right: Either<&str, &str> = Right("right");
assert_eq!(right.left_or("left"), "left");
```

# Report in eyre - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/eyre/0.6.12/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/eyre/struct.Report.html

`pub struct Report { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

The core error reporting type of the library, a wrapper around a dynamic error reporting type.

`Report` works a lot like `Box<dyn std::error::Error>`, but with these
differences:

- `Report`requires that the error is- `Send`,- `Sync`, and- `'static`.
- `Report`guarantees that a backtrace is available, even if the underlying error type does not provide one.
- `Report`is represented as a narrow pointer — exactly one word in size instead of two.

[§](https://docs.rs#display-representations)Display representations

When you print an error object using “{}” or to_string(), only the outermost underlying error is printed, not any of the lower level causes. This is exactly as if you had called the Display impl of the error from which you constructed your eyre::Report.

`Failed to read instrs from ./path/to/instrs.json`To print causes as well using eyre’s default formatting of causes, use the alternate selector “{:#}”.

`Failed to read instrs from ./path/to/instrs.json: No such file or directory (os error 2)`The Debug format “{:?}” includes your backtrace if one was captured. Note
that this is the representation you get by default if you return an error
from `fn main` instead of printing it explicitly yourself.

```
Error: Failed to read instrs from ./path/to/instrs.json
Caused by:
    No such file or directory (os error 2)
Stack backtrace:
   0: <E as eyre::context::ext::StdError>::ext_report
             at /git/eyre/src/backtrace.rs:26
   1: core::result::Result<T,E>::map_err
             at /git/rustc/src/libcore/result.rs:596
   2: eyre::context::<impl eyre::WrapErr<T,E,H> for core::result::Result<T,E>>::wrap_err_with
             at /git/eyre/src/context.rs:58
   3: testing::main
             at src/main.rs:5
   4: std::rt::lang_start
             at /git/rustc/src/libstd/rt.rs:61
   5: main
   6: __libc_start_main
   7: _start
```
To see a conventional struct-style Debug representation, use “{:#?}”.

```
Error {
    msg: "Failed to read instrs from ./path/to/instrs.json",
    source: Os {
        code: 2,
        kind: NotFound,
        message: "No such file or directory",
    },
}
```
If none of the built-in representations are appropriate and you would prefer
to render the error and its cause chain yourself, it can be done by defining
your own [ EyreHandler](https://docs.rs/trait.EyreHandler.html) and

[to use it.](https://docs.rs/fn.set_hook.html)

`hook`## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Create a new error object from any error type.

The error type must be threadsafe and `'static`, so that the `Report`
will be as well.

If the error type does not provide a backtrace, a backtrace will be created here to ensure that a backtrace exists.

Create a new error object from a printable error message.

If the argument implements std::error::Error, prefer `Report::new`
instead which preserves the underlying error’s cause chain and
backtrace. If the argument may or may not implement std::error::Error
now or in the future, use `eyre!(err)` which handles either way
correctly.

`Report::msg("...")` is equivalent to `eyre!("...")` but occasionally
convenient in places where a function is preferable over a macro, such
as iterator or stream combinators:

```
use eyre::{Report, Result};
use futures::stream::{Stream, StreamExt, TryStreamExt};
async fn demo<S>(stream: S) -> Result<Vec<Output>>
where
    S: Stream<Item = Input>,
{
    stream
        .then(ffi::do_some_work) // returns Result<Output, &str>
        .map_err(Report::msg)
        .try_collect()
        .await
}
```
Create a new error from an error message to wrap the existing error.

For attaching a higher level error message to a `Result` as it is propagated, the
[ WrapErr](https://docs.rs/trait.WrapErr.html) extension trait may be more convenient than this function.

The primary reason to use `error.wrap_err(...)` instead of `result.wrap_err(...)` via the
`WrapErr` trait would be if the message needs to depend on some data held by the underlying
error:

```
use eyre::Result;
use std::fs::File;
use std::path::Path;
struct ParseError {
    line: usize,
    column: usize,
}
fn parse_impl(file: File) -> Result<T, ParseError> {
    ...
}
pub fn parse(path: impl AsRef<Path>) -> Result<T> {
    let file = File::open(&path)?;
    parse_impl(file).map_err(|error| {
        let message = format!(
            "only the first {} lines of {} are valid",
            error.line, path.as_ref().display(),
        );
        eyre::Report::new(error).wrap_err(message)
    })
}
```
An iterator of the chain of source errors contained by this Report.

This iterator will visit every error in the cause chain of this error object, beginning with the error that this error object was created from.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use eyre::Report;
use std::io;
pub fn underlying_io_error_kind(error: &Report) -> Option<io::ErrorKind> {
    for cause in error.chain() {
        if let Some(io_error) = cause.downcast_ref::<io::Error>() {
            return Some(io_error.kind());
        }
    }
    None
}
```
Returns true if `E` is the type held by this error object.

For errors constructed from messages, this method returns true if `E` matches the type of
the message `D` **or** the type of the error on which the message has been attached. For
details about the interaction between message and downcasting, [see here](https://docs.rs/trait.WrapErr.html#effect-on-downcasting).

Attempt to downcast the error object to a concrete type.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/eyre/error.rs.html#424-435)#### pub fn [downcast_ref](https://docs.rs#method.downcast_ref)<E>(&self) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[&E](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/eyre/error.rs.html#424-435)

#### pub fn [downcast_ref](https://docs.rs#method.downcast_ref)<E>(&self) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[&E](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html)>

Downcast this error object by reference.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-1)Example

```
// If the error was caused by redaction, then return a tombstone instead
// of the content.
match root_cause.downcast_ref::<DataStoreError>() {
    Some(DataStoreError::Censored(_)) => Ok(Poll::Ready(REDACTED_CONTENT)),
    None => Err(error),
}
```

# hashbrown - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/hashbrown/

## Expand description

This crate is a Rust port of Google’s high-performance [SwissTable](https://abseil.io/blog/20180927-swisstables) hash
map, adapted to make it a drop-in replacement for Rust’s standard `HashMap`
and `HashSet` types.

The original C++ version of [SwissTable](https://abseil.io/blog/20180927-swisstables) can be found [here](https://github.com/abseil/abseil-cpp/blob/master/absl/container/internal/raw_hash_set.h), and this
[CppCon talk](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ncHmEUmJZf4) gives an overview of how the algorithm works.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [hash_](https://docs.rs/hash_map/index.html)- map
- A hash map implemented with quadratic probing and SIMD lookup.
- [hash_](https://docs.rs/hash_set/index.html)- set
- A hash set implemented as a `HashMap`where the value is`()`.
- [hash_](https://docs.rs/hash_table/index.html)- table
- A hash table implemented with quadratic probing and SIMD lookup.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Default](https://docs.rs/struct.DefaultHashBuilder.html)- Hash - Builder
- Default hash builder for the `S`type parameter of`HashMap``HashSet`
- [Default](https://docs.rs/struct.DefaultHasher.html)- Hasher
- Default hasher for `HashMap``HashSet`
- [HashMap](https://docs.rs/struct.HashMap.html)
- A hash map implemented with quadratic probing and SIMD lookup.
- [HashSet](https://docs.rs/struct.HashSet.html)
- A hash set implemented as a `HashMap`where the value is`()`.
- [Hash](https://docs.rs/struct.HashTable.html)- Table
- Low-level hash table with explicit hashing.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [TryReserve](https://docs.rs/enum.TryReserveError.html)- Error
- The error type for `try_reserve`methods.

# indexmap - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/indexmap/

## Expand description

[ IndexMap](https://docs.rs/map/struct.IndexMap.html) is a hash table where the iteration order of the key-value
pairs is independent of the hash values of the keys.

[ IndexSet](https://docs.rs/set/struct.IndexSet.html) is a corresponding hash set using the same implementation and
with similar properties.

[§](https://docs.rs#highlights)Highlights

[ IndexMap](https://docs.rs/map/struct.IndexMap.html) and

[are drop-in compatible with the std](https://docs.rs/set/struct.IndexSet.html)

`IndexSet``HashMap`
and `HashSet`, but they also have some features of note:- The ordering semantics (see their documentation for details)
- Sorting methods and the `.pop()`
- The `Equivalent`
- The `MutableKeys``MutableValues`

[§](https://docs.rs#feature-flags)Feature Flags

To reduce the amount of compiled code in the crate by default, certain
features are gated behind [feature flags](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/manifest.html#the-features-section). These allow you to opt in to (or
out of) functionality. Below is a list of the features available in this
crate.

- `std`: Enables features which require the Rust standard library. For more information see the section on- `no_std`
- `rayon`: Enables parallel iteration and other parallel methods.
- `serde`: Adds implementations for- `Serialize`- `Deserialize`- `IndexMap`- `IndexSet`- `IndexMap`- `map::serde_seq`
- `arbitrary`: Adds implementations for the- `arbitrary::Arbitrary`- `IndexMap`- `IndexSet`
- `quickcheck`: Adds implementations for the- `quickcheck::Arbitrary`- `IndexMap`- `IndexSet`
- `borsh`(- **deprecated**): Adds implementations for- `BorshSerialize`- `BorshDeserialize`- `IndexMap`- `IndexSet`- `borsh`- `indexmap`,- `borsh v1.5.6`added an- `indexmap`feature that should be used instead of enabling the feature here.

*Note: only the  std feature is enabled by default.*

[§](https://docs.rs#alternate-hashers)Alternate Hashers

[ IndexMap](https://docs.rs/map/struct.IndexMap.html) and

[have a default hasher type](https://docs.rs/set/struct.IndexSet.html)

`IndexSet`[, just like the standard](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/hash/random/struct.RandomState.html)

`S = RandomState``HashMap` and `HashSet`, which is resistant to
HashDoS attacks but not the most performant. Type aliases can make it easier
to use alternate hashers:```
use fnv::FnvBuildHasher;
use indexmap::{IndexMap, IndexSet};
type FnvIndexMap<K, V> = IndexMap<K, V, FnvBuildHasher>;
type FnvIndexSet<T> = IndexSet<T, FnvBuildHasher>;
let std: IndexSet<i32> = (0..100).collect();
let fnv: FnvIndexSet<i32> = (0..100).collect();
assert_eq!(std, fnv);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#rust-version)Rust Version

This version of indexmap requires Rust 1.85 or later.

The indexmap 2.x release series will use a carefully considered version upgrade policy, where in a later 2.x version, we will raise the minimum required Rust version.

[§](https://docs.rs#no-standard-library-targets)No Standard Library Targets

This crate supports being built without `std`, requiring `alloc` instead.
This is chosen by disabling the default “std” cargo feature, by adding
`default-features = false` to your dependency specification.

- Creating maps and sets using `new``with_capacity``std`. Use methods`IndexMap::default``with_hasher``with_capacity_and_hasher``twox-hash`.
- Macros `indexmap!``indexset!``std`. Use the macros`indexmap_with_default!``indexset_with_default!`
